questions.question_text: The number of the real roots of the equation $(x+1)^{2}+|x-5|=\frac{27}{4}$ is ________.
questions.question_html: The number of the real roots of the equation $(x+1)^{2}+|x-5|=\frac{27}{4}$ is ________.
questions.explanation_text: When $x>5$ $(x+1)^{2}+(x-5)=\frac{27}{4}$ $\Rightarrow x^{2}+3x-4=\frac{27}{4}$ $\Rightarrow x^{2}+3x-\frac{43}{4}=0$ $\Rightarrow 4x^{2}+12x-43=0$ $x=\frac{-12 \pm \sqrt{144+688}}{8}$ $x=\frac{-12 \pm \sqrt{832}}{8}=\frac{-12 \pm 28.8}{8}$ $=\frac{-3+7.2}{2}$ $=\frac{-3+7.2}{2},\frac{-3-7.2}{2}$ = 2.1, -5.1 [ both are rejected as x should be > 5 ] (Therefore no solution) For $x \le 5$ $(x+1)^{2}-(x-5)=\frac{27}{4}$ $x^{2}+x+6-\frac{27}{4}=0$ $4x^{2}+4x-3=0$ $x=\frac{-4 \pm \sqrt{16+48}}{8}$ $x=\frac{-4 \pm 8}{8} \Rightarrow x=-\frac{12}{8},\frac{4}{8}$ $\therefore$ So, the equation have two real roots.
questions.explanation_html:
When $x>5$

$(x+1)^{2}+(x-5)=\frac{27}{4}$

$\Rightarrow x^{2}+3x-4=\frac{27}{4}$

$\Rightarrow x^{2}+3x-\frac{43}{4}=0$

$\Rightarrow 4x^{2}+12x-43=0$

$x=\frac{-12 \pm \sqrt{144+688}}{8}$

$x=\frac{-12 \pm \sqrt{832}}{8}=\frac{-12 \pm 28.8}{8}$

$=\frac{-3+7.2}{2}$

$=\frac{-3+7.2}{2},\frac{-3-7.2}{2}$

= 2.1, -5.1 [ both are rejected as x should be > 5 ]

(Therefore no solution)

For $x \le 5$

$(x+1)^{2}-(x-5)=\frac{27}{4}$

$x^{2}+x+6-\frac{27}{4}=0$

$4x^{2}+4x-3=0$

$x=\frac{-4 \pm \sqrt{16+48}}{8}$

$x=\frac{-4 \pm 8}{8} \Rightarrow x=-\frac{12}{8},\frac{4}{8}$

$\therefore$ So, the equation have two real roots.

questions.explanation_text: $e^{6x}-e^{4x}-2e^{3x}-12e^{2x}+e^{x}+1=0$ $\Rightarrow (e^{3x}-1)^{2}-e^{x}(e^{3x}-1)=12e^{2x}$ $(e^{3x}-1)^{2}(e^{x}-e^{-x}-e^{-2x})=12$ $\Rightarrow \underset{increasing(letf(x))}{\underset{}{e^{x}-e^{-x}-e^{-2x}}}=\frac{12}{\underset{decreasing(letg(x))}{\underset{}{e^{3x}-1}}}$ $\Rightarrow$ No. of real roots = 2

questions.question_text: Let $\lambda$ $\ne$ 0 be in R. If $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are the roots of the equation x 2 $-$ x + 2 $\lambda$ = 0, and $\alpha$ and $\gamma$ are the roots of equation 3x 2 $-$ 10x + 27 $\lambda$ = 0, then $\frac{\beta\gamma}{\lambda}$ is equal to ____________.

questions.explanation_text: 3 $\alpha$ 2 $-$ 10 $\alpha$ + 27 $\lambda$ = 0 ..... (1) $\alpha$ 2 $-$ $\alpha$ + 2 $\lambda$ = 0 ...... (2) (1) $-$ 3(2) gives $-$ 7 $\alpha$ + 21 $\lambda$ = 0 $\Rightarrow$ $\alpha$ = 3 $\lambda$ Put $\alpha$ = 3 $\lambda$ in equation (1) we get 9 $\lambda$ 2 $-$ 3 $\lambda$ + 2 $\lambda$ $-$ 0 9 $\lambda$ 2 = $\lambda$ $\Rightarrow$ $\lambda$ = $\frac{1}{9}$ as $\lambda$ $\ne$ 0 Now, $\alpha$ = 3 $\lambda$ $\Rightarrow$ $\lambda$ = $\frac{1}{3}$ $\alpha$ + $\beta$ = 1 $\Rightarrow$ $\beta$ = 2/3 $\alpha$ + $\gamma$ = $\frac{10}{3}$ $\Rightarrow$ $\gamma$ = 3 $\frac{\beta\gamma}{\lambda}=\frac{\frac{2}{3} \times 3}{\frac{1}{9}}=18$
questions.explanation_html:
3 $\alpha$ 2 $-$ 10 $\alpha$ + 27 $\lambda$ = 0 ..... (1)

$\alpha$ 2 $-$ $\alpha$ + 2 $\lambda$ = 0 ...... (2)

(1) $-$ 3(2) gives

$-$ 7 $\alpha$ + 21 $\lambda$ = 0 $\Rightarrow$ $\alpha$ = 3 $\lambda$

Put $\alpha$ = 3 $\lambda$ in equation (1) we get

9 $\lambda$ 2 $-$ 3 $\lambda$ + 2 $\lambda$ $-$ 0

9 $\lambda$ 2 = $\lambda$ $\Rightarrow$ $\lambda$ = $\frac{1}{9}$ as $\lambda$ $\ne$ 0

Now, $\alpha$ = 3 $\lambda$ $\Rightarrow$ $\lambda$ = $\frac{1}{3}$

$\alpha$ + $\beta$ = 1 $\Rightarrow$ $\beta$ = 2/3

$\alpha$ + $\gamma$ = $\frac{10}{3}$ $\Rightarrow$ $\gamma$ = 3

$\frac{\beta\gamma}{\lambda}=\frac{\frac{2}{3} \times 3}{\frac{1}{9}}=18$

questions.question_html: If $\alpha$ , $\beta$ are roots of the equation $x^{2}+5(\sqrt{2})x+10=0$ , $\alpha$ > $\beta$ and $P_{n}=\alpha^{n}-\beta^{n}$ for each positive integer n, then the value of $(\frac{P_{17}P_{20}+5\sqrt{2}P_{17}P_{19}}{P_{18}P_{19}+5\sqrt{2}P_{18}^{2}})$ is equal to _________.
questions.explanation_html:
$x^{2}+5\sqrt{2}x+10=0$

& $P_{n}=\alpha^{n}-\beta^{n}$ (Given)

Now, $\frac{P_{17}P_{20}+5\sqrt{2}P_{17}P_{19}}{P_{18}P_{19}+5\sqrt{2}P_{18}^{2}}$ = $\frac{P_{17}(P_{20}+5\sqrt{2}P_{19})}{P_{18}(P_{19}+5\sqrt{2}P_{18})}$

$\frac{P_{17}(\alpha^{20}-\beta^{20}+5\sqrt{2}(\alpha^{19}-\beta^{19}))}{P_{18}(\alpha^{19}-\beta^{19}+5\sqrt{2}(\alpha^{18}-\beta^{18}))}$

$\frac{P_{17}(\alpha^{19}(\alpha+5\sqrt{2})-\beta^{19}(\beta+5\sqrt{2}))}{P_{18}(\alpha^{18}(\alpha+5\sqrt{2})-\beta^{18}(\beta+5\sqrt{2}))}$

Since, $\alpha+5\sqrt{2}=-10/\alpha$ ..... (1)

& $\beta+5\sqrt{2}=-10/\beta$ ....... (2)

Now, put there values in above expression $=-\frac{10P_{17}P_{18}}{-10P_{18}P_{17}}=1$

questions.question_html: Let $\alpha$ and $\beta$ be the roots of x2 $-$ 6x $-$ 2 = 0. If an = $\alpha$ n $-$ $\beta$ n for n $\ge$ 1, then the value of $\frac{a_{10}-2a_{8}}{3a_{9}}$ is :
questions.explanation_text: Given, $\alpha$ and $\beta$ be the roots of $x^{2}-6x-2=0$ $\begin{aligned} \alpha+\beta=6 \\ \alpha\beta=-2 \end{aligned}$ and $\alpha^{2}-6\alpha-2=0 \Rightarrow \alpha^{2}-2=6\alpha$ $\beta^{2}-6\beta-2=0 \Rightarrow \beta^{2}-2=6\beta$ $\frac{a_{10}-2a_{8}}{3a_{9}}=\frac{(\alpha^{10}-\beta^{10})-2(\alpha^{8}-\beta^{8})}{3(\alpha^{9}-\beta^{9})}$ $=\frac{(\alpha^{10}-2\alpha^{8})-(\beta^{10}-2\beta^{8})}{3(\alpha^{9}-\beta^{9})}$ Now, $=\frac{\alpha^{8}(\alpha^{2}-2)-\beta^{8}(\beta^{2}-2)}{3(\alpha^{9}-\beta^{9})}$ $=\frac{\alpha^{8}(6\alpha)-\beta^{8}(6\beta)}{3(\alpha^{9}-\beta^{9})}=\frac{6(\alpha^{9}-\beta^{9})}{3(\alpha^{9}-\beta^{9})}=\frac{6}{3}=2$
questions.explanation_html:
Given, $\alpha$ and $\beta$ be the roots of $x^{2}-6x-2=0$

$\begin{aligned} \alpha+\beta=6 \\ \alpha\beta=-2 \end{aligned}$

and $\alpha^{2}-6\alpha-2=0 \Rightarrow \alpha^{2}-2=6\alpha$

$\beta^{2}-6\beta-2=0 \Rightarrow \beta^{2}-2=6\beta$

$\frac{a_{10}-2a_{8}}{3a_{9}}=\frac{(\alpha^{10}-\beta^{10})-2(\alpha^{8}-\beta^{8})}{3(\alpha^{9}-\beta^{9})}$

$=\frac{(\alpha^{10}-2\alpha^{8})-(\beta^{10}-2\beta^{8})}{3(\alpha^{9}-\beta^{9})}$

Now, $=\frac{\alpha^{8}(\alpha^{2}-2)-\beta^{8}(\beta^{2}-2)}{3(\alpha^{9}-\beta^{9})}$

$=\frac{\alpha^{8}(6\alpha)-\beta^{8}(6\beta)}{3(\alpha^{9}-\beta^{9})}=\frac{6(\alpha^{9}-\beta^{9})}{3(\alpha^{9}-\beta^{9})}=\frac{6}{3}=2$

questions.explanation_text: $\frac{2}{x-1}-\frac{1}{x-2}=\frac{2}{k}$ $x \in R-{1,2}$ $\Rightarrow k(2x-4-x+1)=2(x^{2}-3x+2)$ $\Rightarrow k(x-3)=2(x^{2}-3x+2)$ for x $\ne$ 3, $k=2(x-3+\frac{2}{x-3}+3)$ $x-3+\frac{2}{x-3} \ge 2\sqrt{2},∀x>3$ & $x-3+\frac{2}{x-3} \le -2\sqrt{2},∀x<-3$ $\Rightarrow 2(x-3+\frac{2}{x-3}+3) \in (-\infty,6-4\sqrt{2}]∪[6+4\sqrt{2},\infty)$ for no real roots $k \in (6-4\sqrt{2},6+4\sqrt{2})-{0}$ Integral k $\in$ {1, 2 ..... 11} Sum of k = 66
questions.explanation_html:
$\frac{2}{x-1}-\frac{1}{x-2}=\frac{2}{k}$

$x \in R-{1,2}$

$\Rightarrow k(2x-4-x+1)=2(x^{2}-3x+2)$

$\Rightarrow k(x-3)=2(x^{2}-3x+2)$

for x $\ne$ 3, $k=2(x-3+\frac{2}{x-3}+3)$

$x-3+\frac{2}{x-3} \ge 2\sqrt{2},∀x>3$

& $x-3+\frac{2}{x-3} \le -2\sqrt{2},∀x<-3$

$\Rightarrow 2(x-3+\frac{2}{x-3}+3) \in (-\infty,6-4\sqrt{2}]∪[6+4\sqrt{2},\infty)$

for no real roots

$k \in (6-4\sqrt{2},6+4\sqrt{2})-{0}$

Integral k $\in$ {1, 2 ..... 11}

Sum of k = 66

questions.explanation_text: Given, $\alpha$ + $\beta$ = 1, $\alpha$ $\beta$ = $-$ 1 $\therefore$ Quadratic equation with roots $\alpha$ , $\beta$ is x 2 $-$ x $-$ 1 = 0 $\Rightarrow$ $\alpha$ 2 = $\alpha$ + 1 Multiplying both sides by $\alpha$ n $-$ 1 $\alpha$ n $+$ 1 = $\alpha$ n + $\alpha$ n $-$ 1 ......(1) Similarly, $\beta$ n + 1 = $\beta$ n + $\beta$ n + 1 ..... (2) Adding (1) & (2) $\alpha^{n+1}+\beta^{n+1}=(\alpha^{n}+\beta^{n})+(\alpha^{n-1}+\beta^{n-1})$ $\Rightarrow$ P n+1 = P n + P n $-$ 1 $\Rightarrow$ 29 = P n + 11 (Given, P n + 1 = 29, P n $-$ 1 = 11) $\Rightarrow$ P n = 18 $\therefore$ $P_{n}^{2}$ = 18 2 = 324
questions.explanation_html:
Given, $\alpha$ + $\beta$ = 1, $\alpha$ $\beta$ = $-$ 1

$\therefore$ Quadratic equation with roots $\alpha$ , $\beta$ is x2 $-$ x $-$ 1 = 0

$\Rightarrow$ $\alpha$ 2 = $\alpha$ + 1

Multiplying both sides by $\alpha$ n $-$ 1

$\alpha$ n $+$ 1 = $\alpha$ n + $\alpha$ n $-$ 1 ......(1)

Similarly,

$\beta$ n + 1 = $\beta$ n + $\beta$ n + 1 ..... (2)

Adding (1) & (2)

$\alpha^{n+1}+\beta^{n+1}=(\alpha^{n}+\beta^{n})+(\alpha^{n-1}+\beta^{n-1})$

$\Rightarrow$ Pn+1 = Pn + Pn $-$ 1

$\Rightarrow$ 29 = Pn + 11 (Given, Pn + 1 = 29, Pn $-$ 1 = 11)

$\Rightarrow$ Pn = 18

$\therefore$ $P_{n}^{2}$ = 182 = 324
key_formulas: 1 = 11 and p n+1 = 29 for some integer n

questions.question_text: If $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are the distinct roots of the equation $x^{2}+(3)^{1/4}x+3^{1/2}=0$ , then the value of $\alpha^{96}(\alpha^{12}-1)+\beta^{96}(\beta^{12}-1)$ is equal to :
questions.question_html: If $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are the distinct roots of the equation $x^{2}+(3)^{1/4}x+3^{1/2}=0$ , then the value of $\alpha^{96}(\alpha^{12}-1)+\beta^{96}(\beta^{12}-1)$ is equal to :
questions.explanation_text: As, $(\alpha^{2}+\sqrt{3})=-(3)^{1/4}.\alpha$ $\Rightarrow (\alpha^{4}+2\sqrt{3}\alpha^{2}+3)=\sqrt{3}\alpha^{2}$ (On squaring) $\therefore$ $(\alpha^{4}+3)=(-)\sqrt{3}\alpha^{2}$ $\Rightarrow \alpha^{8}+6\alpha^{4}+9=3\alpha^{4}$ (Again squaring) $\therefore$ $\alpha^{8}+3\alpha^{4}+9=0$ $\Rightarrow \alpha^{8}=-9-3\alpha^{4}$ (Multiply by $\alpha$ 4 ) So, $\alpha^{12}=-9\alpha^{4}-3\alpha^{8}$ $\therefore$ $\alpha^{12}=-9\alpha^{4}-3(-9-3\alpha^{4})$ $\Rightarrow \alpha^{12}=-9\alpha^{4}+27+9\alpha^{4}$ Hence, $\alpha^{12}=(27)^{2}$ $\Rightarrow (\alpha^{12})^{8}=(27)^{8}$ $\Rightarrow \alpha^{96}=(3)^{24}$ Similarly $\beta^{96}=(3)^{24}$ $\therefore$ $\alpha^{96}(\alpha^{12}-1)+\beta^{96}(\beta^{12}-1)=(3)^{24} \times 52$ $\Rightarrow$ Option (3) is correct.
questions.explanation_html:
As, $(\alpha^{2}+\sqrt{3})=-(3)^{1/4}.\alpha$

$\Rightarrow (\alpha^{4}+2\sqrt{3}\alpha^{2}+3)=\sqrt{3}\alpha^{2}$ (On squaring)

$\therefore$ $(\alpha^{4}+3)=(-)\sqrt{3}\alpha^{2}$

$\Rightarrow \alpha^{8}+6\alpha^{4}+9=3\alpha^{4}$ (Again squaring)

$\therefore$ $\alpha^{8}+3\alpha^{4}+9=0$

$\Rightarrow \alpha^{8}=-9-3\alpha^{4}$

(Multiply by $\alpha$ 4)

So, $\alpha^{12}=-9\alpha^{4}-3\alpha^{8}$

$\therefore$ $\alpha^{12}=-9\alpha^{4}-3(-9-3\alpha^{4})$

$\Rightarrow \alpha^{12}=-9\alpha^{4}+27+9\alpha^{4}$

Hence, $\alpha^{12}=(27)^{2}$

$\Rightarrow (\alpha^{12})^{8}=(27)^{8}$

$\Rightarrow \alpha^{96}=(3)^{24}$

Similarly $\beta^{96}=(3)^{24}$

$\therefore$ $\alpha^{96}(\alpha^{12}-1)+\beta^{96}(\beta^{12}-1)=(3)^{24} \times 52$

$\Rightarrow$ Option (3) is correct.

questions.question_html: Let a, b $\in$ R, a $\ne$ 0 be such that the equation, ax2 – 2bx + 5 = 0 has a repeated root $\alpha$ , which is also a root of the equation, x2 – 2bx – 10 = 0. If $\beta$ is the other root of this equation, then $\alpha$ 2 + $\beta$ 2 is equal to :
questions.explanation_text: Roots of equation ax 2 – 2bx + 5 = 0 are $\alpha$ , $\alpha$ . $\therefore$ $\alpha$ + $\alpha$ = $\frac{2b}{a}$ $\Rightarrow$ 2 $\alpha$ = $\frac{2b}{a}$ $\Rightarrow$ $\alpha$ = $\frac{b}{a}$ ....(1) and $\alpha$ 2 = $\frac{5}{a}$ ....(2) From (1) and (2), we get $\frac{b^{2}}{a^{2}}=\frac{5}{a}$ $\Rightarrow$ b 2 = 5a $\alpha$ , $\beta$ are the roots of equation x 2 – 2bx – 10 = 0 $\therefore$ $\alpha$ + $\beta$ = 2b and $\alpha$ $\beta$ = -10 As $\alpha$ is a root of the equation x 2 – 2bx – 10 = 0. $\therefore$ $\alpha$ 2 - 2b $\alpha$ - 10 = 0 $\Rightarrow$ $\frac{b^{2}}{a^{2}}-\frac{2b^{2}}{a}-10=0$ $\Rightarrow$ $\frac{5a}{a^{2}}-\frac{10a}{a}-10=0$ $\Rightarrow$ $\frac{5}{a}-10-10=0$ $\Rightarrow$ $a$ = $\frac{1}{4}$ $\Rightarrow$ $\alpha^{2}$ = 20 $\alpha$ $\beta$ = -10 $\Rightarrow$ $\beta^{2}$ = 5 $\therefore$ $\alpha^{2}+\beta^{2}$ = 20 + 5 = 25
questions.explanation_html:
Roots of equation ax2 – 2bx + 5 = 0 are $\alpha$ , $\alpha$ .

$\therefore$ $\alpha$ + $\alpha$ = $\frac{2b}{a}$

$\Rightarrow$ 2 $\alpha$ = $\frac{2b}{a}$

$\Rightarrow$ $\alpha$ = $\frac{b}{a}$ ....(1)

and $\alpha$ 2 = $\frac{5}{a}$ ....(2)

From (1) and (2), we get

$\frac{b^{2}}{a^{2}}=\frac{5}{a}$

$\Rightarrow$ b2 = 5a

$\alpha$ , $\beta$ are the roots of equation x2 – 2bx – 10 = 0

$\therefore$ $\alpha$ + $\beta$ = 2b

and $\alpha$ $\beta$ = -10

As $\alpha$ is a root of the equation x2 – 2bx – 10 = 0.

$\therefore$ $\alpha$ 2 - 2b $\alpha$ - 10 = 0

$\Rightarrow$ $\frac{b^{2}}{a^{2}}-\frac{2b^{2}}{a}-10=0$

$\Rightarrow$ $\frac{5a}{a^{2}}-\frac{10a}{a}-10=0$

$\Rightarrow$ $\frac{5}{a}-10-10=0$

$\Rightarrow$ $a$ = $\frac{1}{4}$

$\Rightarrow$ $\alpha^{2}$ = 20

$\alpha$ $\beta$ = -10

$\Rightarrow$ $\beta^{2}$ = 5

$\therefore$ $\alpha^{2}+\beta^{2}$ = 20 + 5 = 25

questions.question_html:
Let $\alpha$ and $\beta$ be the roots of the equation x2 - x - 1 = 0.
If pk = $(\alpha)^{k}+(\beta)^{k}$ , k $\ge$ 1, then which one of the following statements is not true?

options.label: A
options.html: (p1 + p2 + p3 + p4 + p5) = 26

options.label: C
options.html: p3 = p5 – p4

options.label: D
options.html: p5 = p2 · p3

questions.explanation_text: x 2 - x - 1 = 0 $\therefore$ $\alpha$ 2 - $\alpha$ - 1 = 0 $\Rightarrow$ $\alpha$ 2 = $\alpha$ + 1 $\therefore$ $\alpha$ 3 = $\alpha$ 2 + $\alpha$ = $\alpha$ + 1 + $\alpha$ = 2 $\alpha$ + 1 Now $\alpha$ 4 = 2 $\alpha$ 2 + $\alpha$ = 2( $\alpha$ + 1) + $\alpha$ = 3 $\alpha$ + 2 Now $\alpha$ 5 = 3 $\alpha$ 2 + 2 $\alpha$ = 3( $\alpha$ + 1) + 2 $\alpha$ = 5 $\alpha$ + 3 Given p k = $(\alpha)^{k}+(\beta)^{k}$ $\therefore$ p 5 = $(\alpha)^{5}+(\beta)^{5}$ = 5 $\alpha$ + 3 + 5 $\beta$ + 3 = 5( $\alpha$ + $\beta$ ) + 6 = 5(1) + 6 [As $\alpha$ + $\beta$ = 1] = 11 Now p 2 · p 3 = ( $\alpha$ 2 + $\beta$ 2 ).( $\alpha$ 3 + $\beta$ 3 ) = ( $\alpha$ + 1 + $\beta$ + 1)(2 $\alpha$ + 1 + 2 $\beta$ + 1) = ( $\alpha$ + $\beta$ + 2)(2( $\alpha$ + $\beta$ ) + 2) = (1 + 2)(2 + 2) = 12 $\therefore$ p 5 $\ne$ p 2 ·p 3 So option (D) is wrong.
questions.explanation_html:
x2 - x - 1 = 0

$\therefore$ $\alpha$ 2 - $\alpha$ - 1 = 0

$\Rightarrow$ $\alpha$ 2 = $\alpha$ + 1

$\therefore$ $\alpha$ 3 = $\alpha$ 2 + $\alpha$

= $\alpha$ + 1 + $\alpha$

= 2 $\alpha$ + 1

Now $\alpha$ 4 = 2 $\alpha$ 2 + $\alpha$

= 2( $\alpha$ + 1) + $\alpha$

= 3 $\alpha$ + 2

Now $\alpha$ 5 = 3 $\alpha$ 2 + 2 $\alpha$

= 3( $\alpha$ + 1) + 2 $\alpha$

= 5 $\alpha$ + 3

Given pk = $(\alpha)^{k}+(\beta)^{k}$

$\therefore$ p5 = $(\alpha)^{5}+(\beta)^{5}$

= 5 $\alpha$ + 3 + 5 $\beta$ + 3

= 5( $\alpha$ + $\beta$ ) + 6

= 5(1) + 6 [As $\alpha$ + $\beta$ = 1]

= 11

Now p2 · p3

= ( $\alpha$ 2 + $\beta$ 2).( $\alpha$ 3 + $\beta$ 3)

= ( $\alpha$ + 1 + $\beta$ + 1)(2 $\alpha$ + 1 + 2 $\beta$ + 1)

= ( $\alpha$ + $\beta$ + 2)(2( $\alpha$ + $\beta$ ) + 2)

= (1 + 2)(2 + 2) = 12

$\therefore$ p5 $\ne$ p2 ·p3

So option (D) is wrong.

questions.question_html:
Let $\lambda \ne 0$ be in R. If $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are the roots of the
equation, x2 - x + 2 $\lambda$ = 0 and $\alpha$ and $\gamma$ are the roots of
the equation, $3x^{2}-10x+27\lambda=0$ , then $\frac{\beta\gamma}{\lambda}$ is equal to:
questions.explanation_text: $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are the roots of the equation x 2 - x + 2 $\lambda$ = 0 .....(1) $\therefore$ $\alpha+\beta=1,\alpha\beta=2\lambda$ $\alpha$ and $\gamma$ are the roots of the equation, $3x^{2}-10x+27\lambda=0$ ......(2) $\therefore$ $\alpha+\gamma$ = $\frac{10}{3}$ , $\alpha\gamma$ = $\frac{27\lambda}{3}$ = 9 $\lambda$ Multiplying equation (1) by 3 and subtracting form equation (2) we get -7x + 21 $\lambda$ = 0 $\Rightarrow$ x = 3 $\lambda$ $\therefore$ $\alpha$ = 3 $\lambda$ As $\alpha$ is root of equation (1) so $\alpha$ 2 - $\alpha$ + 2 $\lambda$ = 0 $\Rightarrow$ 9 $\lambda$ 2 - 3 $\lambda$ + 2 $\lambda$ = 0 $\Rightarrow$ $\lambda$ = $\frac{1}{9}$ $\Rightarrow$ $\alpha$ = 3 $\times$ $\frac{1}{9}$ = $\frac{1}{3}$ Also $\alpha\beta=2\lambda$ = $\frac{2}{9}$ $\Rightarrow$ $\beta$ = $\frac{2}{3}$ Also $\alpha\gamma$ = 9 $\lambda$ = 9 $\times$ $\frac{1}{9}$ = 1 $\Rightarrow$ $\gamma$ = 3 $\therefore$ $\frac{\beta\gamma}{\lambda}$ = $\frac{\frac{2}{3}.3}{\frac{1}{9}}$ = 18
questions.explanation_html:
$\alpha$ and $\beta$ are the roots of the
equation x2 - x + 2 $\lambda$ = 0 .....(1)

$\therefore$ $\alpha+\beta=1,\alpha\beta=2\lambda$

$\alpha$ and $\gamma$ are the roots of
the equation, $3x^{2}-10x+27\lambda=0$ ......(2)

$\therefore$ $\alpha+\gamma$ = $\frac{10}{3}$ , $\alpha\gamma$ = $\frac{27\lambda}{3}$ = 9 $\lambda$

Multiplying equation (1) by 3 and subtracting form equation (2) we get

-7x + 21 $\lambda$ = 0

$\Rightarrow$ x = 3 $\lambda$

$\therefore$ $\alpha$ = 3 $\lambda$

As $\alpha$ is root of equation (1) so

$\alpha$ 2 - $\alpha$ + 2 $\lambda$ = 0

$\Rightarrow$ 9 $\lambda$ 2 - 3 $\lambda$ + 2 $\lambda$ = 0

$\Rightarrow$ $\lambda$ = $\frac{1}{9}$

$\Rightarrow$ $\alpha$ = 3 $\times$ $\frac{1}{9}$ = $\frac{1}{3}$

Also $\alpha\beta=2\lambda$ = $\frac{2}{9}$

$\Rightarrow$ $\beta$ = $\frac{2}{3}$

Also $\alpha\gamma$ = 9 $\lambda$ = 9 $\times$ $\frac{1}{9}$ = 1

$\Rightarrow$ $\gamma$ = 3

$\therefore$ $\frac{\beta\gamma}{\lambda}$ = $\frac{\frac{2}{3}.3}{\frac{1}{9}}$ = 18

questions.question_html:

$(\alpha-\frac{1}{\alpha})(\beta-\frac{1}{\beta})(\alpha+\frac{1}{\beta})(\beta+\frac{1}{\alpha})$ is equal to :
questions.explanation_text:
$\alpha$ and $\beta$ are the roots of the equation
x 2 + px + 2 = 0 $\therefore$ $\alpha+\beta=-p,\alpha\beta=2$ $\frac{1}{\alpha}$ and $\frac{1}{\beta}$ are the roots of
the equation 2x 2 + 2qx + 1 = 0 $\therefore$ $\frac{1}{\alpha}+\frac{1}{\beta}=-q,\frac{1}{\alpha\beta}=\frac{1}{2}$ $\Rightarrow$ $\frac{\alpha+\beta}{\alpha\beta}=-q \Rightarrow \frac{-p}{2}=-q$ $\Rightarrow p=2q$ $(\alpha+\frac{1}{\beta})(\beta+\frac{1}{\alpha})=\alpha\beta+\frac{1}{\alpha\beta}+2$ $=2+\frac{1}{2}+2=\frac{9}{2}$ $(\alpha-\frac{1}{\alpha})(\beta-\frac{1}{\beta})=\alpha\beta+\frac{1}{\alpha\beta}-\frac{\alpha}{\beta}-\frac{\beta}{\alpha}$ $=2+\frac{1}{2}-[\frac{\alpha^{2}+\beta^{2}}{\alpha\beta}]$ $=\frac{5}{2}-[\frac{(\alpha+\beta)^{2}-2\alpha\beta}{\alpha\beta}]$ $=\frac{5}{2}-[\frac{p^{2}-4}{2}]$ $=\frac{9-p^{2}}{2}$ $(\alpha-\frac{1}{\alpha})(\beta-\frac{1}{\beta})(\alpha+\frac{1}{\beta})(\beta+\frac{1}{\alpha})=(\frac{9-p^{2}}{2})(\frac{9}{2})$ $=\frac{9}{4}(9-p^{2})$
questions.explanation_html:
$\alpha$ and $\beta$ are the roots of the

equation x2 + px + 2 = 0

$\therefore$ $\alpha+\beta=-p,\alpha\beta=2$

$\frac{1}{\alpha}$ and $\frac{1}{\beta}$ are the roots of the

equation 2x2 + 2qx + 1 = 0

$\therefore$ $\frac{1}{\alpha}+\frac{1}{\beta}=-q,\frac{1}{\alpha\beta}=\frac{1}{2}$

$\Rightarrow$ $\frac{\alpha+\beta}{\alpha\beta}=-q \Rightarrow \frac{-p}{2}=-q$

$\Rightarrow p=2q$

$(\alpha+\frac{1}{\beta})(\beta+\frac{1}{\alpha})=\alpha\beta+\frac{1}{\alpha\beta}+2$ $=2+\frac{1}{2}+2=\frac{9}{2}$

$(\alpha-\frac{1}{\alpha})(\beta-\frac{1}{\beta})=\alpha\beta+\frac{1}{\alpha\beta}-\frac{\alpha}{\beta}-\frac{\beta}{\alpha}$

$=2+\frac{1}{2}-[\frac{\alpha^{2}+\beta^{2}}{\alpha\beta}]$ $=\frac{5}{2}-[\frac{(\alpha+\beta)^{2}-2\alpha\beta}{\alpha\beta}]$

$=\frac{5}{2}-[\frac{p^{2}-4}{2}]$

$=\frac{9-p^{2}}{2}$

$(\alpha-\frac{1}{\alpha})(\beta-\frac{1}{\beta})(\alpha+\frac{1}{\beta})(\beta+\frac{1}{\alpha})=(\frac{9-p^{2}}{2})(\frac{9}{2})$

$=\frac{9}{4}(9-p^{2})$

questions.question_text: Let $\alpha$ and $\beta$ be the roots of x 2 - 3x + p=0 and $\gamma$ and $\delta$ be the roots of x 2 - 6x + q = 0. If $\alpha,\beta,\gamma,\delta$ form a geometric progression.Then ratio (2q + p) : (2q - p) is:
questions.question_html: Let $\alpha$ and $\beta$ be the roots of x2 - 3x + p=0 and $\gamma$ and $\delta$ be the roots of x2 - 6x + q = 0. If $\alpha,\beta,\gamma,\delta$ form a geometric progression.Then ratio (2q + p) : (2q - p) is:
questions.explanation_text: $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are the roots of x 2 $-$ 3x + p = 0 $\therefore$ $\alpha$ + $\beta$ = 3 and $\alpha\beta$ = p $\gamma$ and $\delta$ are the roots of x 2 $-$ 6x + q = 0 $\therefore$ $\gamma$ + $\delta$ = 6 and $\gamma\delta$ = q Given that, $\alpha$ , $\beta$ , $\gamma$ , $\delta$ are in G.P. $\therefore$ Let $\alpha$ = a, $\beta$ = ar, $\gamma$ = ar 2 and $\delta$ = ar 3 As $\alpha$ + $\beta$ = 3 $\Rightarrow$ a + ar = 3 $\Rightarrow$ a(1 + r) = 3 ...(1) Also $\gamma$ + $\delta$ = 6 $\Rightarrow$ ar 2 + ar 3 = 6 $\Rightarrow$ ar 2 (1 + r) = 6 ... (2) Dividing (2) by (1), r 2 = 2 $\Rightarrow r=\sqrt{2}$ $\therefore$ $a=\frac{3}{1+\sqrt{2}}$ So, $\alpha=\frac{3}{1+\sqrt{2}}$ , $\beta=\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{1+\sqrt{2}}$ , $\gamma=\frac{3 \times 2}{1+\sqrt{2}}$ , $\delta=\frac{3(2\sqrt{2)}}{1+\sqrt{2}}$ $\therefore$ $p=\alpha\beta=\frac{9\sqrt{2}}{(1+\sqrt{2})^{2}}$ and $q=\gamma\delta=\frac{36\sqrt{2}}{(1+\sqrt{2})^{2}}$ Now, $\frac{2q+p}{2q-p}$ $=\frac{\frac{72\sqrt{2}}{(1+\sqrt{2})^{2}}+\frac{9\sqrt{2}}{(1+\sqrt{2})^{2}}}{\frac{72\sqrt{2}}{(1+\sqrt{2})^{2}}-\frac{9\sqrt{2}}{(1+\sqrt{2})^{2}}}$ $=\frac{72\sqrt{2}+9\sqrt{2}}{72\sqrt{2}-9\sqrt{2}}$ $=\frac{81}{63}$ $=\frac{9}{7}$
questions.explanation_html:
$\alpha$ and $\beta$ are the roots of x2 $-$ 3x + p = 0

$\therefore$ $\alpha$ + $\beta$ = 3 and $\alpha\beta$ = p

$\gamma$ and $\delta$ are the roots of x2 $-$ 6x + q = 0

$\therefore$ $\gamma$ + $\delta$ = 6 and $\gamma\delta$ = q

Given that, $\alpha$ , $\beta$ , $\gamma$ , $\delta$ are in G.P.

$\therefore$ Let $\alpha$ = a, $\beta$ = ar, $\gamma$ = ar2 and $\delta$ = ar3

As $\alpha$ + $\beta$ = 3

$\Rightarrow$ a + ar = 3

$\Rightarrow$ a(1 + r) = 3 ...(1)

Also $\gamma$ + $\delta$ = 6

$\Rightarrow$ ar2 + ar3 = 6

$\Rightarrow$ ar2 (1 + r) = 6 ... (2)

Dividing (2) by (1),

r2 = 2

$\Rightarrow r=\sqrt{2}$

$\therefore$ $a=\frac{3}{1+\sqrt{2}}$

So, $\alpha=\frac{3}{1+\sqrt{2}}$ , $\beta=\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{1+\sqrt{2}}$ , $\gamma=\frac{3 \times 2}{1+\sqrt{2}}$ , $\delta=\frac{3(2\sqrt{2)}}{1+\sqrt{2}}$

$\therefore$ $p=\alpha\beta=\frac{9\sqrt{2}}{(1+\sqrt{2})^{2}}$

and $q=\gamma\delta=\frac{36\sqrt{2}}{(1+\sqrt{2})^{2}}$

Now, $\frac{2q+p}{2q-p}$

$=\frac{\frac{72\sqrt{2}}{(1+\sqrt{2})^{2}}+\frac{9\sqrt{2}}{(1+\sqrt{2})^{2}}}{\frac{72\sqrt{2}}{(1+\sqrt{2})^{2}}-\frac{9\sqrt{2}}{(1+\sqrt{2})^{2}}}$

$=\frac{72\sqrt{2}+9\sqrt{2}}{72\sqrt{2}-9\sqrt{2}}$

$=\frac{81}{63}$

$=\frac{9}{7}$

questions.question_text: If $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are the roots of the quadratic equation, x 2 + x sin $\theta$ - 2 sin $\theta$ = 0, $\theta \in (0,\frac{\pi}{2})$ , then $\frac{\alpha^{12}+\beta^{12}}{(\alpha^{-12}+\beta^{-12}).(\alpha-\beta)^{24}}$ is equal to :
questions.question_html:
If $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are the roots of the quadratic equation,
x2 + x sin $\theta$ - 2 sin $\theta$ = 0, $\theta \in (0,\frac{\pi}{2})$ , then
$\frac{\alpha^{12}+\beta^{12}}{(\alpha^{-12}+\beta^{-12}).(\alpha-\beta)^{24}}$ is equal to :
questions.explanation_text: Given $\alpha+\beta=-sin\theta$ and $\alpha\beta=-2sin\theta$ $\frac{(\alpha^{12}+\beta^{12})\alpha^{12}\beta^{12}}{(\alpha^{12}+\beta^{12})(\alpha-\beta)^{24}}=\frac{(\alpha\beta)^{12}}{(\alpha-\beta)^{24}}$ $|\alpha-\beta|=\sqrt{(\alpha+\beta)^{2}-4\alpha\beta}=\sqrt{sin^{2}\theta+8sin\theta}$ Hence required quantity $\frac{(\alpha\beta)^{12}}{(\alpha-\beta)^{24}}=\frac{(2sin\theta)^{12}}{sin^{12}\theta(sin\theta+8)^{12}}=\frac{2^{12}}{(sin\theta+8)^{12}}$
questions.explanation_html:
Given $\alpha+\beta=-sin\theta$ and $\alpha\beta=-2sin\theta$

$\frac{(\alpha^{12}+\beta^{12})\alpha^{12}\beta^{12}}{(\alpha^{12}+\beta^{12})(\alpha-\beta)^{24}}=\frac{(\alpha\beta)^{12}}{(\alpha-\beta)^{24}}$

$|\alpha-\beta|=\sqrt{(\alpha+\beta)^{2}-4\alpha\beta}=\sqrt{sin^{2}\theta+8sin\theta}$

Hence required quantity

$\frac{(\alpha\beta)^{12}}{(\alpha-\beta)^{24}}=\frac{(2sin\theta)^{12}}{sin^{12}\theta(sin\theta+8)^{12}}=\frac{2^{12}}{(sin\theta+8)^{12}}$

questions.question_text: The sum of the solutions of the equation $|\sqrt{x}-2|+\sqrt{x}(\sqrt{x}-4)+2=0$ (x > 0) is equal to:
questions.question_html:
The sum of the solutions of the equation
$|\sqrt{x}-2|+\sqrt{x}(\sqrt{x}-4)+2=0$
(x > 0) is equal to:
questions.explanation_text: Case 1 : When $\sqrt{x} \ge 2$ then $|\sqrt{x}-2|=\sqrt{x}-2$ $\therefore$ The given equation becomes, $(\sqrt{x}-2)$ + $\sqrt{x}(\sqrt{x}-4)+2$ = 0 $\Rightarrow$ $(\sqrt{x}-2)$ + $x-4\sqrt{x}$ + 2 = 0 $\Rightarrow$ $x-3\sqrt{x}$ = 0 $\Rightarrow$ $\sqrt{x}(\sqrt{x}-3)$ = 0 $\therefore$ $\sqrt{x}$ = 0 or 3 $\sqrt{x}$ = 0 is not possible as $\sqrt{x} \ge 2$ . So, $\sqrt{x}$ = 3 or $x$ = 9 Case 2 : When $\sqrt{x}<2$ then $|\sqrt{x}-2|=$ $-(\sqrt{x}-2)$ = $2-\sqrt{x}$ $\therefore$ The given equation becomes, $(2-\sqrt{x})$ + $\sqrt{x}(\sqrt{x}-4)+2$ = 0 $\Rightarrow$ $2-\sqrt{x}$ + $x-4\sqrt{x}$ + 2 = 0 $\Rightarrow$ $x-5\sqrt{x}+4$ = 0 $\Rightarrow$ $x-4\sqrt{x}-\sqrt{x}+4$ = 0 $\Rightarrow$ $\sqrt{x}(\sqrt{x}-4)$ $-(\sqrt{x}-4)$ = 0 $\Rightarrow$ $(\sqrt{x}-4)$ $(\sqrt{x}-1)$ = 0 $\therefore$ $\sqrt{x}$ = 4 or 1 $\sqrt{x}$ = 4 is not possible as $\sqrt{x}<2$ . $\therefore$ $\sqrt{x}$ = 1 or $x$ = 1 So, Sum of all solutions = 9 + 1 = 10
questions.explanation_html:
Case 1 : When $\sqrt{x} \ge 2$

then $|\sqrt{x}-2|=\sqrt{x}-2$

$\therefore$ The given equation becomes,

$(\sqrt{x}-2)$ + $\sqrt{x}(\sqrt{x}-4)+2$ = 0

$\Rightarrow$ $(\sqrt{x}-2)$ + $x-4\sqrt{x}$ + 2 = 0

$\Rightarrow$ $x-3\sqrt{x}$ = 0

$\Rightarrow$ $\sqrt{x}(\sqrt{x}-3)$ = 0

$\therefore$ $\sqrt{x}$ = 0 or 3

$\sqrt{x}$ = 0 is not possible as $\sqrt{x} \ge 2$ .

So, $\sqrt{x}$ = 3

or $x$ = 9

Case 2 : When $\sqrt{x}<2$

then $|\sqrt{x}-2|=$ $-(\sqrt{x}-2)$ = $2-\sqrt{x}$

$\therefore$ The given equation becomes,

$(2-\sqrt{x})$ + $\sqrt{x}(\sqrt{x}-4)+2$ = 0

$\Rightarrow$ $2-\sqrt{x}$ + $x-4\sqrt{x}$ + 2 = 0

$\Rightarrow$ $x-5\sqrt{x}+4$ = 0

$\Rightarrow$ $x-4\sqrt{x}-\sqrt{x}+4$ = 0

$\Rightarrow$ $\sqrt{x}(\sqrt{x}-4)$ $-(\sqrt{x}-4)$ = 0

$\Rightarrow$ $(\sqrt{x}-4)$ $(\sqrt{x}-1)$ = 0

$\therefore$ $\sqrt{x}$ = 4 or 1

$\sqrt{x}$ = 4 is not possible as $\sqrt{x}<2$ .

$\therefore$ $\sqrt{x}$ = 1

or $x$ = 1

So, Sum of all solutions = 9 + 1 = 10

questions.question_text:
If $\alpha$ , $\beta$ and $\gamma$ are three consecutive terms of a non-constant G.P. such that the equations $\alpha$ x 2 + 2 $\beta$ x + $\gamma$ = 0 and
x 2 + x – 1 = 0 have a common root, then $\alpha$ ( $\beta$ + $\gamma$ ) is equal to :
questions.question_html: If $\alpha$ , $\beta$ and $\gamma$ are three consecutive terms of a non-constant G.P. such that the equations $\alpha$ x 2 + 2 $\beta$ x + $\gamma$ = 0 and x2 + x – 1 = 0 have a common root, then $\alpha$ ( $\beta$ + $\gamma$ ) is equal to :
questions.explanation_text: Let the common ratio of G.P is r Then the equation of $\alpha x^{2}+2\beta x+\gamma=0$ $\Rightarrow$ $\alpha x^{2}+2\alpha rx+\alpha r^{2}=0$ $\Rightarrow$ x 2 + 2rx + r 2 = 0 ........ (i) Equation (i) and x 2 + x - 1 = 0 ......... (ii) has a common root. Now (i) - (ii) $\Rightarrow$ (2r-1)x + (r 2 +1) = 0 $\Rightarrow$ x = $\frac{-(r^{2}+1)}{2r-1}$ ....... (iii) Now putting (iii) in equation (ii) $\Rightarrow$ (r 2 +1) 2 - (r 2 +1) (2r - 1) - (2r - 1) 2 = 0 $\Rightarrow$ r 4 - 2r 3 - r 2 + 2r + 1 = 0 .......... (iv) dividing equation (iv) by r 2 $\Rightarrow$ r 2 - 2r - 1 + $\frac{2}{r}+\frac{1}{r^{2}}=0$ $\Rightarrow$ $(r-\frac{1}{r})^{2}-2(r-\frac{1}{r})+1=0$ $\Rightarrow$ $(r-\frac{1}{r}-r)^{2}=0$ $\Rightarrow$ $\frac{r^{2}-1}{r}=1$ $\Rightarrow$ r 2 = 1 + r Now $\alpha$ ( $\beta$ + $\gamma$ ) $\Rightarrow$ $\alpha$ ( $\alpha$ r + $\alpha$ r 2 ) $\Rightarrow$ $\alpha^{2}r(1+r)$ [ $\because$ r 2 = 1 + r] $\Rightarrow$ $\alpha^{2}r.r^{2}$ $\Rightarrow$ $(\alpha r)(\alpha r^{2})$ $\Rightarrow$ $\beta$ $\gamma$
questions.explanation_html:
Let the common ratio of G.P is r

Then the equation of $\alpha x^{2}+2\beta x+\gamma=0$

$\Rightarrow$ $\alpha x^{2}+2\alpha rx+\alpha r^{2}=0$

$\Rightarrow$ x2 + 2rx + r2 = 0 ........(i)
Equation (i) and x2 + x - 1 = 0 ......... (ii) has a common root.

Now (i) - (ii) $\Rightarrow$ (2r-1)x + (r2+1) = 0

$\Rightarrow$ x = $\frac{-(r^{2}+1)}{2r-1}$ ....... (iii)

Now putting (iii) in equation (ii)

$\Rightarrow$ (r2+1)2 - (r2+1) (2r - 1) - (2r - 1)2 = 0

$\Rightarrow$ r4 - 2r3 - r2 + 2r + 1 = 0 .......... (iv)

dividing equation (iv) by r2

$\Rightarrow$ r2 - 2r - 1 + $\frac{2}{r}+\frac{1}{r^{2}}=0$

$\Rightarrow$ $(r-\frac{1}{r})^{2}-2(r-\frac{1}{r})+1=0$

$\Rightarrow$ $(r-\frac{1}{r}-r)^{2}=0$

$\Rightarrow$ $\frac{r^{2}-1}{r}=1$ $\Rightarrow$ r2 = 1 + r

Now $\alpha$ ( $\beta$ + $\gamma$ ) $\Rightarrow$ $\alpha$ ( $\alpha$ r + $\alpha$ r2)

$\Rightarrow$ $\alpha^{2}r(1+r)$   [ $\because$ r2 = 1 + r]

$\Rightarrow$ $\alpha^{2}r.r^{2}$ $\Rightarrow$ $(\alpha r)(\alpha r^{2})$ $\Rightarrow$ $\beta$ $\gamma$

questions.question_html:
If m is chosen in the quadratic equation

(m2 + 1) x2 – 3x + (m2 + 1)2 = 0

such that the sum of its roots is greatest, then the absolute difference of the cubes of its roots is :-
questions.explanation_text:
Given quadratic equation (m 2 + 1)
x 2 – 3x + (m 2 + 1) 2 = 0 Let roots of the equation $\alpha$ and $\beta$ . $\therefore$ Sum of roots = $\alpha$ + $\beta$ = $\frac{3}{m^{2}+1}$ Product of roots = $\alpha$ $\beta$ = m 2 + 1 $\frac{3}{m^{2}+1}$ is maximum when m = 0 Hence equation becomes x 2 – 3x + 1 = 0 $\alpha+\beta=3$ , $\alpha\beta=1$ $|\alpha-\beta|$ = $\sqrt{(\alpha+\beta)^{2}-4\alpha\beta}$ = $\sqrt{(3)^{2}-4.1}$ = $\sqrt{5}$ $|\alpha^{3}-\beta^{3}|=|(\alpha-\beta)(\alpha^{2}+\beta^{2}+\alpha\beta)|$ = $\sqrt{5}|(\alpha+\beta)^{2}-\alpha\beta|$ $=\sqrt{5}(9-1)=8\sqrt{5}$
questions.explanation_html:
Given quadratic equation

(m2 + 1) x2 – 3x + (m2 + 1)2 = 0

Let roots of the equation $\alpha$ and $\beta$ .

$\therefore$ Sum of roots = $\alpha$ + $\beta$ = $\frac{3}{m^{2}+1}$

Product of roots = $\alpha$ $\beta$ = m2 + 1

$\frac{3}{m^{2}+1}$ is maximum when m = 0

Hence equation becomes x2 – 3x + 1 = 0

$\alpha+\beta=3$ ,    $\alpha\beta=1$   

$|\alpha-\beta|$ = $\sqrt{(\alpha+\beta)^{2}-4\alpha\beta}$ = $\sqrt{(3)^{2}-4.1}$ = $\sqrt{5}$

$|\alpha^{3}-\beta^{3}|=|(\alpha-\beta)(\alpha^{2}+\beta^{2}+\alpha\beta)|$

= $\sqrt{5}|(\alpha+\beta)^{2}-\alpha\beta|$

$=\sqrt{5}(9-1)=8\sqrt{5}$

options.label: D
options.html: p2 + q2 + r2

questions.explanation_text: Given, $\frac{1}{x+p}+\frac{1}{x+q}=\frac{1}{r}$ $\Rightarrow$ $\frac{x+p+x+q}{(x+p)(x+q)}=\frac{1}{r}$ $\Rightarrow$ (2x + p + q) r = x 2 + px + qx + pq $\Rightarrow$ x 2 + (p + q $-$ 2r) x + pq $-$ pr $-$ qr = 0 Let $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are the roots, $\therefore$ $\alpha$ + $\beta$ = $-$ (p + q $-$ 2r) and $\alpha$ $\beta$ = pq $-$ pr $-$ qr Given that, $\alpha$ = $-$ $\beta$ $\Rightarrow$ $\alpha$ + $\beta$ = 0 $\therefore$ $-$ (p + q $-$ 2r) = 0 Now, $\alpha$ 2 + $\beta$ 2 = ( $\alpha$ + $\beta$ ) 2 $-$ 2 $\alpha$ $\beta$ = ( $-$ (p + q $-$ 2r)) 2 $-$ 2 (pq $-$ pr $-$ qr) = p 2 +q 2 + 4r 2 + 2pq $-$ 4pr $-$ 4qr $-$ 2pq + 2pr + 2qr = p 2 + q 2 + 4r 2 $-$ 2pr $-$ 2qr = p 2 + q 2 $-$ 2r (p + q $-$ 2r) = p 2 + q 2 $-$ 2r (0) = p 2 + q 2
questions.explanation_html:
Given,

$\frac{1}{x+p}+\frac{1}{x+q}=\frac{1}{r}$

$\Rightarrow$ $\frac{x+p+x+q}{(x+p)(x+q)}=\frac{1}{r}$

$\Rightarrow$ (2x + p + q) r = x2 + px + qx + pq

$\Rightarrow$ x2 + (p + q $-$ 2r) x + pq $-$ pr $-$ qr = 0

Let $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are the roots,

$\therefore$ $\alpha$ + $\beta$ = $-$ (p + q $-$ 2r)

and $\alpha$ $\beta$ = pq $-$ pr $-$ qr

Given that, $\alpha$ = $-$ $\beta$ $\Rightarrow$ $\alpha$ + $\beta$ = 0

$\therefore$ $-$ (p + q $-$ 2r) = 0

Now, $\alpha$ 2 + $\beta$ 2

= ( $\alpha$ + $\beta$ )2 $-$ 2 $\alpha$ $\beta$

= ( $-$ (p + q $-$ 2r))2 $-$ 2 (pq $-$ pr $-$ qr)

= p2 +q2 + 4r2 + 2pq $-$ 4pr $-$ 4qr $-$ 2pq + 2pr + 2qr

= p2 + q2 + 4r2 $-$ 2pr $-$ 2qr

= p2 + q2 $-$ 2r (p + q $-$ 2r)

= p2 + q2 $-$ 2r (0)

= p2 + q2

questions.explanation_text: Given, $2|\sqrt{x}-3|+\sqrt{x}(\sqrt{x}-6)+6=0$ Case 1 : When $\sqrt{x}-3 \ge 0,$ then equation becomes $2(\sqrt{x}-3)+\sqrt{x}(\sqrt{x}-6)+6=0$ $\Rightarrow 2\sqrt{x}-6+x-6\sqrt{x}+6=0$ $\Rightarrow x-4\sqrt{x}=0$ $\Rightarrow \sqrt{x}(\sqrt{x}-4)=0$ $\therefore$ $\sqrt{x}=0,4$ but as $\sqrt{x}-3 \ge 0$ or $\sqrt{x} \ge 3$ then $\sqrt{x} \ne 0$ $\therefore$ $\sqrt{x}=4$ value is possible. Case 2 : When $\sqrt{x}-3<0$ or $\sqrt{x}<3.$ There equation becomes $-2(\sqrt{x}-3)+\sqrt{x}(\sqrt{x}-6)+6=0$ $\Rightarrow -2\sqrt{x}+6+x-6\sqrt{x}+6=0$ $\Rightarrow x-8\sqrt{x}+12=0$ $\Rightarrow x-6\sqrt{x}-2\sqrt{x}+12=0$ $\Rightarrow \sqrt{x}(\sqrt{x}-6)-2(\sqrt{x}-6)=0$ $\Rightarrow (\sqrt{x}-2)(\sqrt{x}-6)=0$ $\therefore$ $\sqrt{x}=2,6$ as $\sqrt{x}<3$ so $\sqrt{x} \ne 6$ $\therefore$ $\sqrt{x}=2$ is possible. So, total possible value of $\sqrt{x}=2,4$ or for x possible values are 4, 16. $\therefore$ Set S contains exactly two elements 4 and 16.

When $\sqrt{x}-3 \ge 0,$ then equation becomes

$\Rightarrow 2\sqrt{x}-6+x-6\sqrt{x}+6=0$

$\Rightarrow x-4\sqrt{x}=0$

$\Rightarrow \sqrt{x}(\sqrt{x}-4)=0$

$\therefore$ $\sqrt{x}=0,4$

but as $\sqrt{x}-3 \ge 0$ or $\sqrt{x} \ge 3$ then $\sqrt{x} \ne 0$

$\therefore$ $\sqrt{x}=4$ value is possible.

Case 2 :

When $\sqrt{x}-3<0$ or $\sqrt{x}<3.$ There equation becomes

$-2(\sqrt{x}-3)+\sqrt{x}(\sqrt{x}-6)+6=0$

$\Rightarrow -2\sqrt{x}+6+x-6\sqrt{x}+6=0$

$\Rightarrow x-8\sqrt{x}+12=0$

$\Rightarrow x-6\sqrt{x}-2\sqrt{x}+12=0$

$\Rightarrow \sqrt{x}(\sqrt{x}-6)-2(\sqrt{x}-6)=0$

$\Rightarrow (\sqrt{x}-2)(\sqrt{x}-6)=0$

$\therefore$ $\sqrt{x}=2,6$

as $\sqrt{x}<3$ so $\sqrt{x} \ne 6$

$\therefore$ $\sqrt{x}=2$ is possible.

So, total possible value of $\sqrt{x}=2,4$

or for x possible values are 4, 16.

$\therefore$ Set S contains exactly two elements 4 and 16.

questions.explanation_text: $\sum_{r=1}^{n}(x+r-1)(x+r)=10n$ $\Rightarrow$ $\sum_{r=1}^{n}(x^{2}+xr+(r-1)x+r^{2}-r)=10n$ $\Rightarrow$ $\sum_{r=1}^{n}(x^{2}+(2r-1)x+r(r-1))=10n$ $\Rightarrow$ $nx^{2}+{1+3+5+....+(2n-1)}x$ $+{1.2+2.3+...+(n-1)n}$ = 10n $\Rightarrow$ $nx^{2}+n^{2}x+\frac{n(n^{2}-1)}{3}=10n$ $\Rightarrow$ $x^{2}+nx+\frac{(n^{2}-31)}{3}=0$ Let $\alpha$ and $\alpha$ + 1 be its two solutions $\therefore$ $\alpha$ + ( $\alpha$ + 1) = -n $\Rightarrow$ $\alpha$ = $\frac{-n-1}{2}$ ....(1) Also $\alpha$ ( $\alpha$ + 1) = $\frac{(n^{2}-31)}{3}$ ......(2) Putting value of (1) in (2), we get $-(\frac{n+1}{2})(\frac{1-n}{2})=\frac{(n^{2}-31)}{3}$ $\Rightarrow$ n 2 = 121 $\Rightarrow$ n = 11

questions.question_html: If x is a solution of the equation, $\sqrt{2x+1}$ $-\sqrt{2x-1}=1,$ $(x \ge \frac{1}{2}),$ then $\sqrt{4x^{2}-1}$ is equal to :

Squaring both sides, we get

2x + 1 $=$ 1 + 2x $-$ 1 + 2 $\sqrt{2x-1}$

$\Rightarrow$    8x $-$ 4 $=$ 1

$\Rightarrow$    x $=$ $\frac{5}{8}$

So,     $\sqrt{4x^{2}-1}$

$=\sqrt{4(\frac{25}{64})-1}$

$=\sqrt{\frac{36}{64}}$

$=\frac{6}{8}$

= $\frac{6}{2}$ (as $\alpha+\beta$ = 6)

= 3

questions.explanation_html:
Given, $-3(x-[x])^{2}+2(x-[x])+a^{2}=0$
As we know, $[x]+{x}=x$
where $[x]$ is integral part and ${x}$ is fractional part.
$\therefore$ ${x}=x-[x]$
Now put ${x}$ inplace of $x-[x]$ in the equation.
The new equation is $-3{x}^{2}+2{x}+a^{2}=0$

[Note : Question says this equation has no integral solution, it means ${x} \ne$ 0. So, $x$ is not a integer.]

$\therefore$ ${x}$ = $\frac{-2 \pm \sqrt{4-4 \times (-3)a^{2}}}{-6}$
             = $\frac{-2 \pm \sqrt{4+12a^{2}}}{-6}$
As ${x}$ is fractional part so it is lies between 0 to 1( $0 \le {x}<1$ ).

By considering positive sign, we get

$0 \le \frac{-2+\sqrt{4+12a^{2}}}{-6}<1$

$\Rightarrow$ $0 \ge -2+\sqrt{4+12a^{2}}>-6$

$\Rightarrow$ $2 \ge +\sqrt{4+12a^{2}}>-4$

$\because$ $+\sqrt{4+12a^{2}}$ is always positive which is greater than any negative no. So can ignore the inequality $+\sqrt{4+12a^{2}}>-4$

Consider this inequality,
$2 \ge +\sqrt{4+12a^{2}}$
$\Rightarrow$ $4 \ge 4+12a^{2}$
$\Rightarrow$ $12a^{2} \le 0$
$\Rightarrow$ $a^{2} \le 0$
$\Rightarrow$ $a^{2}=0$
$\Rightarrow$ $a=0$

If $a$ = 0 then $-3{x}^{2}+2{x}=0$ so ${x}$ becomes 0 but question says ${x}$ $\ne$ 0.
So $a$ can't be 0.

Now by considering negative sign, we get


$0 \le \frac{-2-\sqrt{4+12a^{2}}}{-6}<1$

$\Rightarrow$ $0 \ge -2-\sqrt{4+12a^{2}}>-6$

$-\sqrt{4+12a^{2}}>-4$

$\Rightarrow$ $a^{2}<1$

questions.explanation_text: $x^{2}-(a-2)x-a-1=0$ $\Rightarrow \alpha+\beta=a-2;\alpha\beta=-(a+1)$ $\alpha^{2}+\beta^{2}=(\alpha+\beta)^{2}-2\alpha\beta$ $=a^{2}-2a+6=(a-1)^{2}+5$ For min. value of $\alpha^{2}+\beta^{2}$ where $\alpha$ is an integer $\Rightarrow a=1.$
questions.explanation_html:
$x^{2}-(a-2)x-a-1=0$

$\Rightarrow \alpha+\beta=a-2;\alpha\beta=-(a+1)$

$\alpha^{2}+\beta^{2}=(\alpha+\beta)^{2}-2\alpha\beta$

$=a^{2}-2a+6=(a-1)^{2}+5$

For min. value of $\alpha^{2}+\beta^{2}$ where $\alpha$ is an integer

$\Rightarrow a=1.$

questions.explanation_text: $ax^{2}+bx+c=0,$ $\alpha+\beta=\frac{-b}{a},\alpha\beta=\frac{c}{a}$ As for given condition, $\alpha+\beta=\frac{1}{\alpha^{2}}+\frac{1}{\beta^{2}}$ $\alpha+\beta=\frac{\alpha^{2}+\beta^{2}}{\alpha^{2}\beta^{2}}-\frac{b}{a}$ $=\frac{\frac{b^{2}}{a^{2}}-\frac{2c}{a}}{\frac{c^{2}}{a^{2}}}$ On simplification $2a^{2}c=ab^{2}+bc^{2}$ $\Rightarrow \frac{2a}{b}=\frac{c}{a}+\frac{b}{c}$ $\Rightarrow \frac{c}{a},\frac{a}{b},\frac{b}{c}$ are in $A.P.$ $\therefore$ $\frac{a}{c},\frac{b}{a},&$ are in $H.P.$
questions.explanation_html:
$ax^{2}+bx+c=0,$ $\alpha+\beta=\frac{-b}{a},\alpha\beta=\frac{c}{a}$

As for given condition, $\alpha+\beta=\frac{1}{\alpha^{2}}+\frac{1}{\beta^{2}}$

$\alpha+\beta=\frac{\alpha^{2}+\beta^{2}}{\alpha^{2}\beta^{2}}-\frac{b}{a}$

$=\frac{\frac{b^{2}}{a^{2}}-\frac{2c}{a}}{\frac{c^{2}}{a^{2}}}$

On simplification $2a^{2}c=ab^{2}+bc^{2}$

$\Rightarrow \frac{2a}{b}=\frac{c}{a}+\frac{b}{c}$

$\Rightarrow \frac{c}{a},\frac{a}{b},\frac{b}{c}$ are in $A.P.$

$\therefore$ $\frac{a}{c},\frac{b}{a},&$ are in $H.P.$

questions.explanation_text: Let the roots of given equation be $\alpha$ and $2$ $\alpha$ then $\alpha+2\alpha=3\alpha=\frac{1-3a}{a^{2}-5a+3}$ and $\alpha.2\alpha=2\alpha^{2}=\frac{2}{a^{2}-5a+3}$ $\Rightarrow \alpha=\frac{1-3a}{3(a^{2}-5a+3)}$ $\therefore$ $2[\frac{1}{9}\frac{(1-3a)^{2}}{(a^{2}-5a+3)^{2}}]$ $=\frac{2}{a^{2}-5a+3}$ $\frac{(1-3a)^{2}}{(a^{2}-5a+3)}=9$ or $9a^{2}-6a+1$ $=9a^{2}-45a+27$ or $39a=26$ or $a=\frac{2}{3}$

questions.question_html: Difference between the corresponding roots of $x^{2}+ax+b=0$ and $x^{2}+bx+a=0$ is same and $a \ne b,$ then
questions.explanation_text: Let $\alpha,\beta$ and $\gamma,\delta$ be the roots of the equations $x^{2}+ax+b=0$ and $x^{2}+bx+a=0$ respectively. $\therefore$ $\alpha+\beta=-a,\alpha\beta=b$ and $\gamma+\delta=-b,\gamma\delta=a.$ Given $|\alpha-\beta|=|\gamma-\delta|$ $\Rightarrow (\alpha-\beta)^{2}=(\gamma-\delta)^{2}$ $\Rightarrow (\alpha+\beta)^{2}-4\alpha\beta=(\gamma+\delta)^{2}-4\gamma\delta$ $\Rightarrow a^{2}-4b=b^{2}-4a$ $\Rightarrow (a^{2}-b^{2})+4(a-b)=0$ $\Rightarrow a+b+4=0$ ( as $a \ne b$ )
questions.explanation_html:
Let $\alpha,\beta$ and $\gamma,\delta$ be the roots of the equations $x^{2}+ax+b=0$

and $x^{2}+bx+a=0$ respectively.

$\therefore$ $\alpha+\beta=-a,\alpha\beta=b$

and $\gamma+\delta=-b,\gamma\delta=a.$

Given $|\alpha-\beta|=|\gamma-\delta|$

$\Rightarrow (\alpha-\beta)^{2}=(\gamma-\delta)^{2}$

$\Rightarrow (\alpha+\beta)^{2}-4\alpha\beta=(\gamma+\delta)^{2}-4\gamma\delta$

$\Rightarrow a^{2}-4b=b^{2}-4a$

$\Rightarrow (a^{2}-b^{2})+4(a-b)=0$

$\Rightarrow a+b+4=0$

( as $a \ne b$ )

questions.explanation_text: We have $\alpha^{2}=5\alpha-3$ and $\beta^{2}=5\beta-3;$ $\Rightarrow \alpha&\beta$ are roots of equation, $x^{2}=5x-3$ or $x^{2}-5x+3=0$ $\therefore$ $\alpha+\beta=5$ and $\alpha\beta=3$ Thus, the equation having $\frac{\alpha}{\beta}&\frac{\beta}{\alpha}$ as its roots is $x^{2}-x(\frac{\alpha}{\beta}+\frac{\beta}{\alpha})+\frac{\alpha\beta}{\alpha\beta}=0$ $\Rightarrow x^{2}-x(\frac{\alpha^{2}+\beta^{2}}{\alpha\beta})+1=0$ or $3x^{2}-19x+3=0$
questions.explanation_html:
We have $\alpha^{2}=5\alpha-3$ and $\beta^{2}=5\beta-3;$

$\Rightarrow \alpha&\beta$ are roots of

equation, $x^{2}=5x-3$ or $x^{2}-5x+3=0$

$\therefore$ $\alpha+\beta=5$ and $\alpha\beta=3$

Thus, the equation having $\frac{\alpha}{\beta}&\frac{\beta}{\alpha}$ as its roots is

$x^{2}-x(\frac{\alpha}{\beta}+\frac{\beta}{\alpha})+\frac{\alpha\beta}{\alpha\beta}=0$

$\Rightarrow x^{2}-x(\frac{\alpha^{2}+\beta^{2}}{\alpha\beta})+1=0$

or $3x^{2}-19x+3=0$
